This is actually something called prognathism and it's one of the traits we look at when analyzing prehistoric skulls, since as a general rule, evolutionarily, the further back you go in our species, the greater the prognathism. We started as australopithecines with skull shapes very similar to our common chimpanzee ancestor (and also modern chimpanzees) and as we evolved, our chins began to shorten and drop under the maxila, instead of out in front of it.

Coincidentally, the group with the largest degree of prognathism in modern populations is Africans. Interpret that however you like.

I once had to explain the above evolutionary trend to an anthropology lab after we had asked students to collect a class-wide data set of various skull measurements, one of which included prognathism. The fact that a very big, very fat black girl had prognathism outside of 2 standard deviations from the rest of the class made for a rather awkward situation.

But hey, we're FPH. Numbers don't lie.
